Grimbergen
GRIM-bair-gun
n. (the Brabant Premonstratensian abbey of 1128, whose motto is taken from the burning bush)
From Dutch grim, a personal name or a mask, and bergen, hills.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Grimbergen north of Brussels was founded in 1128 and became Premonstratensian within a few years. It was burnt down three times, in 1142, in 1578 during the religious wars, and again in 1797 after the French suppression, and each time the community rebuilt; its baroque church of 1660 is one of the finest in Belgium. The abbey took for its arms a phoenix in flames with the motto Ardet nec consumitur, it burns and is not consumed, which is a Latin quotation of Exodus. This dictionary records Grimbergen for that motto, because the bush is one of the most loaded images in Scripture. Moses turns aside to a fire that does not destroy what it burns, “the bush burned with fire, and the bush was not consumed” (Exo 3:2). God promises the same of his people in flood and flame, “when thou walkest through the fire, thou shalt not be burned” (Isa 43:2). Three men came out of a furnace untouched, “upon whose bodies the fire had no power” (Dan 3:27), and the fire that does come is for refining rather than for ruin, “though it be tried with fire, might be found unto praise and honour” (1Pe 1:7).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a bush as a shrub with branches; to consume as to destroy by burning; a furnace as an enclosed fireplace for intense heat; to refine as to purify from dross; and a trial as a test or examination.

expand to see more

BUSH, n. A shrub with branches; a thick shrub; also, a cluster of shrubs; an assemblage of thick shrubs.

CONSUME, v.t. To destroy by separating the parts of a thing, by decomposition, as by fire, or eating; to destroy utterly.

FURNACE, n. A place where a vehement fire may be made, as for melting ores or metals, or for heating a building.

REFINE, v.t. To purify; to clear from dross, dregs or recrement; as, to refine gold or silver; to purify from what is coarse.

TRIAL, n. Any effort or exertion of strength for the purpose of ascertaining its effect; a test; examination by a test.

Key Scripture

Exo 3:2 — "And the angel of the LORD appeared unto him in a flame of fire out of the midst of a bush: and he looked, and, behold, the bush burned with fire, and the bush was not consumed."

Isa 43:2 — "When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee; and through the rivers, they shall not overflow thee: when thou walkest through the fire, thou shalt not be burned; neither shall the flame kindle upon thee."

Dan 3:27 — "And the princes, governors, and captains, and the king's counsellors, being gathered together, saw these men, upon whose bodies the fire had no power, nor was an hair of their head singed, neither were their coats changed, nor the smell of fire had passed on them."

1Pe 1:7 — "That the trial of your faith, being much more precious than of gold that perisheth, though it be tried with fire, might be found unto praise and honour and glory at the appearing of Jesus Christ:"

Modern Corruption

Brabant Premonstratensian abbey of 1128: burnt three times and rebuilt three times, under a motto taken from the bush that was not consumed.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is what the bush actually showed Moses. The remarkable thing was not the fire but the survival of what it burned, which is why the text says both halves, “the bush burned with fire, and the bush was not consumed” (Exo 3:2). God afterwards applies the figure to his people under judgment and exile, and is careful not to promise the absence of fire, “when thou walkest through the fire, thou shalt not be burned” (Isa 43:2).

The second thing is the distinction between fire that destroys and fire that refines. The three in Nebuchadnezzar's furnace were examined afterwards by a crowd looking for damage and found none, “nor was an hair of their head singed” (Dan 3:27). Peter uses the same figure for ordinary trials, and the point is the metal rather than the heat, “That the trial of your faith, being much more precious than of gold that perisheth” (1Pe 1:7). An abbey burnt three times chose its motto well.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew ceneh (H5572), a bush; Hebrew 'akal (H398), to consume; Hebrew kavah (H3554), to burn; Greek dokimion (G1383), a testing; Greek pur (G4442), fire.

expand to see more

Hebrew ceneh (H5572) — a bush, burning and unburnt; “the bush burned with fire, and the bush was not consumed”, Exodus 3:2.

Hebrew 'akal (H398) — to eat, to consume utterly; “and the bush was not consumed”, Exodus 3:2.

Hebrew kavah (H3554) — to be scorched, which they were not; “thou shalt not be burned”, Isaiah 43:2.

Hebrew charak (H2761) — to singe; not a hair of them; “nor was an hair of their head singed”, Daniel 3:27.

Greek dokimion (G1383) — the proving of a thing by fire; “That the trial of your faith”, 1 Peter 1:7.

Usage

"“the bush burned with fire, and the bush was not consumed” (Exo 3:2) — the motto, in its original."

"“when thou walkest through the fire, thou shalt not be burned” (Isa 43:2) — no promise that there is no fire."

"“That the trial of your faith” (1Pe 1:7) — fire for refining, not for ruin."
